title: The Interview Room
subtitle: A detective, a neighbor who says he took the trash out, and one detail that does not fit.
description: A B1 reading and listening dialogue: a police interview that turns on a single inconsistency, with past continuous practice, detective vocabulary and inference exercises.
passage: Detective Wayne: Good morning, Mr. Rogers. Thank you for coming in. I'd like to start with Sunday night. What were you doing at two in the morning?
Rogers: Good morning, detective. I was waiting up for my favorite show. It airs late.
Detective Wayne: Was anyone with you?
Rogers: My wife, Sharon.
Detective Wayne: Sharon told us she fell asleep at one thirty.
Rogers: That's right. We were watching television and she started snoring. That's how I knew she'd fallen asleep.
Detective Wayne: Your neighbor Philip says he saw you through his window at ten past two. He says you were running down the street.
Rogers: Then he's lying. Philip loves a rumor. He'll repeat anything.
Detective Wayne: Two security cameras on that block agree with him. You were outside on Sunday night, Mr. Rogers. Why did you tell me you weren't?
Rogers: All right — I took the trash out. That's all. It didn't seem worth mentioning.
Detective Wayne: It wasn't worth mentioning. Mrs. Carter was killed on that street while she was walking home, and you were the one person outside.
Rogers: That wasn't me. I swear it wasn't me.
Detective Wayne: Did you see Mrs. Carter while you were out there?
Rogers: Yes. She was arguing with a man near the corner. Tall, dark coat. He looked a lot like Philip, actually.
Detective Wayne: Arguing about what?
Rogers: He was shouting that she'd been seeing someone else. He was furious.
Detective Wayne: And then what did you hear?
Rogers: Gunshots. Two of them. I ran straight back inside and locked the door.
Detective Wayne: Two gunshots.
Rogers: Yes. That's why I was running. Anyone would have run.

Detective Wayne: Mr. Rogers, Mrs. Carter was not shot. There was no firearm on that street on Sunday night, and no neighbor reported a shot — not Philip, not anyone. So I'd like you to tell me again what you heard.
Rogers: I… I may have been mistaken. It was late.
Detective Wayne: You were certain thirty seconds ago. You gave me a number. Would you like to start again, or would you like to call a lawyer first?
Rogers: I think I'd like the lawyer.
Detective Wayne: That's your right. Interview suspended at nine forty-one.

vocabulary.definition: to stay awake instead of going to bed
to be broadcast on television or radio
information passed between people that may not be true
a camera that records a place to prevent or prove crime
to say very seriously that something is true
a person qualified to advise and represent you in law

exercises.title: Following the Interview
exercises.instructions: This is a puzzle as much as a text. Work out what the detective works out.

items.prompt: What was Rogers's first account of his night?
options: That he was asleep beside his wife
That he was awake indoors, waiting for a late television show
That he was walking the neighborhood with Philip
items.explanation: “I was waiting up for my favorite show. It airs late.” He placed himself inside the house.

items.prompt: How did Rogers know Sharon had fallen asleep?
options: She told him she was going to bed
She began snoring while they were watching television
items.explanation: “She started snoring. That's how I knew she'd fallen asleep.”

items.prompt: Why does the camera footage matter so much to the detective?
options: It shows the argument on the corner
It identifies the man in the dark coat
It supports Philip's account, so Rogers's denial collapses
items.explanation: Rogers called Philip a liar, but “two security cameras on that block agree with him” — which is why the detective asks why Rogers denied being outside.

items.prompt: How does Rogers explain being outside once he can no longer deny it?
options: He says he was taking out the trash and it seemed too minor to mention
He says he was looking for his wife
He says he was following Philip
items.explanation: “I took the trash out. That's all. It didn't seem worth mentioning.”

items.prompt: What is the single detail that undoes Rogers's story?
options: He claimed to hear two gunshots, but Mrs. Carter was not shot and no gun was involved
He said Philip was wearing a dark coat
He got the time of the television show wrong
items.explanation: “Mrs. Carter was not shot. There was no firearm on that street.” Rogers described a sound that nobody could have heard.

items.prompt: Why does the detective repeat “Two gunshots” back to him?
options: She did not hear him clearly
She is letting him commit firmly to a detail she already knows is false
She is checking the recording is working
items.explanation: She says afterward, “You were certain thirty seconds ago. You gave me a number.” The repetition pins the claim down before she takes it apart.

items.prompt: What does Rogers's answer “It was late” suggest about him at that moment?
options: That he has a clear memory he is willing to defend
That he is retreating, looking for any explanation for a detail he invented
That he is about to accuse Philip again
items.explanation: He moves from “Two of them” to “I may have been mistaken” in a few seconds — the certainty disappears as soon as it is tested.

items.prompt: Why does the writer end the dialogue where they do?
options: Because the case has been formally closed
Because Rogers has confessed in full
Because Rogers has been caught in a lie but not proved guilty, which leaves the reader to judge
items.explanation: Asking for a lawyer suspends the interview. A lie has been exposed; who killed Mrs. Carter is still open.

exercises.title: True or False?
exercises.instructions: Decide whether each statement is supported by the dialogue.

items.statement: Sharon can confirm where her husband was at two in the morning.
items.explanation: False — she was asleep from one thirty, so she can account for nothing after that.

items.statement: Philip's account turned out to be accurate.
items.explanation: True — the cameras agreed with him, despite Rogers calling him a liar.

items.statement: Rogers admitted straight away that he had gone outside.
items.explanation: False — he admitted it only after being told about the cameras.

items.statement: A neighbor reported hearing a shot that night.
items.explanation: False — “no neighbor reported a shot — not Philip, not anyone”.

items.statement: The detective proves that Rogers killed Mrs. Carter.
items.explanation: False — she proves he lied. The killing is not resolved in the dialogue.

items.statement: Rogers has the right to speak to a lawyer.
items.explanation: True — the detective answers, “That's your right.”

exercises.title: Past Continuous & Past Simple
exercises.instructions: The interview keeps asking what was in progress and what interrupted it. Complete each sentence with the correct form.

items.prompt: What ___ you ___ at two in the morning?
items.explanation: Past continuous for an action in progress at a particular past time: what were you doing?

items.prompt: While we ___ television, she started snoring.
items.explanation: The longer background action takes the past continuous; the sudden one takes the past simple.

items.prompt: Philip says he saw Rogers while he ___ down the street.
items.explanation: Running was in progress when Philip saw him.

items.prompt: Mrs. Carter was killed while she ___ home.
items.explanation: Walking home was interrupted by the killing.

items.prompt: She ___ with a man when Rogers came outside.
items.explanation: The argument was already under way when he arrived.

items.prompt: I ___ straight back inside and ___ the door.
items.explanation: Two completed actions in sequence — both past simple.

discussion: Who do you think killed Mrs. Carter, and what in the dialogue makes you think so?
Rogers lied about something small — taking the trash out. Why do innocent people sometimes lie to the police?
The detective never raises her voice. Is that more effective than shouting? Why?
Continue the story: write about 120 words of the next interview, with Philip in the chair.
